messages.subject: loess curves
messages.body_plain:
Good afternoon,

This is NOT a question about regression analysis. :)

I have created sets of scatterplots in R of position over time -- one set with the Basic R plotting tools and another set with ggplot2. A loess (lowess) curve has been superimposed upon the scatterplot in each. What I'd like to do is model the change on that loess curve. Does anyone have experience with:

1) pulling the loess curve out so that it can be studied directly? I'd ideally like to have some set of x,y points that represent the curve (I think), though the function of the curve itself might be useful.

2) calculating derivatives on that curve and plotting the result? I have various reasons for asking that. I would like to (a), study velocity and acceleration throughout the curve and (b) find turning points on the curve by seeing when the derivative or second derivative = 0. Currently I am visually estimating turning points.

I've found various functions and packages that calculate derivatives in R; however, it is not clear that they are exactly what I want. It is also possible that I myself do not precisely understand what I want. For instance, if I wanted to calculate a set of changes in position over time myself, I am unclear on what set of points to calculate change over? Are there standards?

If anyone is aware of standards or simply tools, I would welcome your knowledge. Some related calculations are commonly done in mouse-tracking work (and indeed I am looking at touch gesture tracking).

Hunter

Hunter Hatfield
Linguistics Programme
University of Otago

Hi Hunter,

> 1) pulling the loess curve out so that it can be studied directly? I'd

R's "lowess" function returns by default the x and y locations of the
fit. You can read more about it by typing "?lowess"

> 2) calculating derivatives on that curve and plotting the result? I
> have various reasons for asking that. I would like to (a), study
> velocity and acceleration throughout the curve and (b) find turning
> points on the curve by seeing when the derivative or second derivative
> = 0. Currently I am visually estimating turning points.

R's "diff" may be what you want here--it will compute N'th order
differences from (for instance) the y values of what is returned from
lowess. I'm sure there are fancier estimators, but I don't know about
them.

Best,

++Steve

messages.subject: Significance and random slopes
messages.body_plain:
Dear R-langers,

In an logistic mixed-effects model I'm working on, I have random intercepts for both subjects and items. Following Barr et al., I make sure to include random slopes for the predictors that I'm theoretically interested in.  While doing so, I find that a particular predictor is significant when random slopes are included for it (grouped by speakers and Items) but it is not significant when these slopes are removed.

I understand from the Barr et al. paper that if you don't include random slopes, you run the chance that p-values may be erroneously low (leading to increased Type I errors). This is what makes me a little surprised by this result because it seems to be working in the opposite direction. Is this behavior expected? 

My second question relates to how to deal with random slopes that cause models to not converge.  I'm interested in seeing if a second predictor is significant when the predictor I mentioned above is already in the model. The problem is that the maximal random effects structure with random slopes for both predictors grouped by subjects and items, fails to converge. It turns out that if I remove the random slope for the second predictor from one of the groupings, the model converges. But now I'm wondering if this will handicap this second predictor in the sense that having a random slope seems to be able to (at least in some cases), lower the p-value.

Thank you,
Ariel Goldberg

messages.subject: error bars based on lmer
messages.body_plain:
Dear list members,

 

How can I use the output of an LMER to generate Error bars for a factorial
design?

 

I have a 2 x 3 design, in which the 3 level factor is a speech continuum
(presented within subjects) coded as covariate (-0.5, 0, 0.5)

and the binary condition coded as -0.5, 0.5.

 

Here is the output:

 

Fixed effects:

                                Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    

(Intercept)          0.5492     0.2680   2.050  0.04041 *  

Continuum        -3.5183     0.3517 -10.002  < 2e-16 ***

Condition             0.4039     0.1341   3.012  0.00260 ** 

Continuum:
Condition            -0.8399     0.2610  -3.218  0.00129 **

 

The analysis shows an effect of exposure, however, if I want to have error
bars
in the graph and I use the standard error of the mean, they are overlapping.

 

This is probably due to the fact that the subjects have a general bias in
how they
perceive the speech continuum, so that the mean is quite variable, but there
is 
clear tendency for all participants to give more /x/ responses in Condition
B compared to Condition A.

(Tyring to keep this generic).

 

So, How can I use the output of the lmer to generate error bars that reflect
the statistical analysis. (obviously I would have to calculate that in
logOdds space
and then re-convert into proportions again for the figure, leading to
asymmetric error bars,
but this is the trivial part). 

 

Kind regards,

Holger

messages.subject: Re: error bars based on lmer
messages.body_plain:
Dear Holger,

you can use this script by Sven Hohenstein from Reinhold Kliegl's group to remove random variance from your dependent variable:

> http://read.psych.uni-potsdam.de/attachments/article/90/remef.v0.6.9.R

The syntax takes some getting-used-to, though. For a model with random intercepts for subjects and items you would simply do (assuming a binomial variable):

> new_dv <- remef(model, ran=list(1,1), family = binomial))

If you have random slopes, I usually find it easier to list the fixed factors (names, no indices) and use keep=TRUE like this:

> new_dv <- remef(model, fix=c('(Intercept)', 'Continuum', 'Condition', 'Continuum:Condition'), keep=TRUE, family = binomial)


Once you have the cleaned-up dependent variable, you can compute confidence intervals and they should no longer overlap (if you see an effect in your model).

Best,
Paul

Dear Paul,

Thanks for your quick reply. I manage to get it to work like this.

1. Getting the new DV with all random slopes (as you described)
new_dv <- remef(aba.lmer, fix=c('(Intercept)', 'steps', 'exposureC',
'steps:exposureC'), keep=TRUE, family = binomial)

2. Applying the qlogis-function to get logOdds

3. aggregating the data frame to the subject level (no items in this
speech-perception exp)

4. getting Mean and SD from this data frame 

5. Getting the standard errors by SE = SD/sqrt(n)

This gives values of around 0.04 logit units, which seems too small to me.
Given the lmer results:

> > Continuum:
> > Condition            -0.8399     0.2610  -3.218  0.00129 **

I had expected something in the vicinity of the Standard Error of the Binary
Effect
(= condition). Somewhere I must be doing something wrong.

Kind regards,
Holger

messages.subject: Announcement: afex 0.6-82 now on CRAN
messages.body_plain:
Dear list members,

With the release of R 3.0.2 and lme 1.0.4, I have pushed
a new version of afex (Analysis of Factorial EXperiments,
version 0.6-82) to CRAN which was accepted yesrterday and
should appear on your CRAN mirror within the next day.

It contains some new features that may be of interest:

- mixed() (for obtaining p-values for LMMs and GLMMs) now
   has method = "LRT" to obtain p-values from likelihood
   ratio tests (via the anova function). This method is
   computationally inexpensive (i.e, fast) and
   recommended by e.g., Barr et al. (2013, JML).

- fitting models in mixed() can now be parallelized using
   a cluster via package parallel (e.g., one can use
   multiple cores on one computer).

(more: http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/afex/NEWS)

Note, mixed() now only works with the new version of
lme4 (>= 1.0.4). If there is interest I will provide a
version that is backwards compatible, so please mail me
if you need such a version.

To use method = "PB", for p-values based on parametric
bootstrap, you will need pbkrtest 0.3-6 which also was
just pushed to CRAN (thanks to Søren Højsgaard).

General infos onm afex here:
http://www.psychologie.uni-freiburg.de/Members/singmann/R/afex

Best,
Henrik

PS: To those also subscribed to R-SIG-mixed, sorry for cross-posting.

-- 
Dipl. Psych. Henrik Singmann
PhD Student
Albert-Ludwigs-Universität Freiburg, Germany
http://www.psychologie.uni-freiburg.de/Members/singmann

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to show a null effect. Traditional p-value is helpless here, 
so I am resorting to the Bayes factor which shows the likelihood of a 
null or alternative effect. I wonder whether anyone has tried this using 
LME results? I found these calculators 
(http://pcl.missouri.edu/bayesfactor) but not sure which one to use 
(regression? I use LME here). Or probably there is a better way of doing 
this on the basis of AIC or BIC?

Thanks for any answer,

Zhenguang Cai

messages.subject: Re: Calculating Bayes factor based on LME
messages.subject_clean: Calculating Bayes factor based on LME
messages.body_plain:
With the little I know, I don't think this is the approach you want.  The
Bayes Factor approach gives you something like a model comparison, which
can imitate an aspect of Bayesian inference, but if you really want strong
evidence that a given effect is null, I think you really need a full-out
Bayesian parameter estimation.  Kruschke's recent tutorial paper on
Bayesian replacement for the t-test (
http://www.indiana.edu/~kruschke/articles/Kruschke2013JEPG.pdf) has a
helpful (at least to a novice like me) discussion in Appendix D.  One of
his points is that low-powered experiments could give a false impression of
"confirming the null" if you just looked at the BF without also looking at
the full posterior.

Alternatively, a good power analysis showing that for a reasonable effect
size you would expect to have found something significant (but didn't) may
be just as convincing to reviewers as a Bayesian analysis, and will
probably take less work to accomplish correctly.

my two cents,
-scott

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Let me chip in for the BayesFactor package as well. It is really extremely convenient and flexible (e.g., allows for crossed-random effects). A helpful introduction can be found at: http://bayesfactorpcl.r-forge.r-project.org/

In addition to BayesFactors for really arbitrary designs, the package even allows you to sample from the posterior distribution to obtain an estimate of the effect (i.e., what Kruschke and Gelman would advocate).

Furthermore, the paper detailing the math behind the package received the Duncan Luce outstanding paper award in 2013 from the Society for Mathematical Psychology: http://pcl.missouri.edu/sites/default/files/Rouder.JMP_.2012.pdf

We have just submitted a paper to PLOS ONE in which we extensively use and describe this package in the domain of human reasoning to find evidence for a null-hypothesis. As a bonus, the supplemental material contains the data and the code to perform the analysis (which includes sampling from the posterior). As the paper is currently right in the submission process I cannot send out a draft through the list but will do so through personal mail if you are interested (which will include the code as well).

Best,
Henrik

PS: The only thing the BayesFactor package is currently lacking is that it doesn't estimate the correlation between random slopes.

> Hi all,
>
> I am trying to show a null effect. Traditional p-value is helpless here, so I am resorting to the Bayes factor which shows the likelihood of a null or alternative effect. I wonder whether anyone has tried this using LME results? I found these calculators (http://pcl.missouri.edu/bayesfactor) but not sure which one to use (regression? I use LME here). Or probably there is a better way of doing this on the basis of AIC or BIC?
>
> Thanks for any answer,
>
> Zhenguang Cai
>

-- 
Dipl. Psych. Henrik Singmann
PhD Student
Albert-Ludwigs-Universität Freiburg, Germany
http://www.psychologie.uni-freiburg.de/Members/singmann
